cia-0000119203:
In August 1968 the CIA compared an unidentified prisoner photograph, numbered 109, with known photos of Roy F. Townley. The task was simple to state and hard to do: decide whether the man in the prisoner photo was Townley. Work like this sat at the center of the prisoner accounting effort.

Photo comparison was painstaking work done from grainy prints and old service pictures. A match could bring a family long-awaited news, while a wrong call could do real harm. The document preserves one such comparison, showing how analysts tried to put names to faces when the prisoners themselves could not be asked.
cia-0000119703:
A September 1952 CIA paper forecasts probable developments in the Union of South Africa. The country was four years into formal apartheid, and its government was tightening racial rule. Analysts in Washington were asked to chart where the country was heading.

Forecast papers like this one weighed a government's strength, its opposition, and the pressures that might change it. South Africa posed hard questions, since it was both an anti-communist partner and a state building open racial rule. The paper records the agency's early read on that problem. It marks the start of a long American effort to judge a regime whose policies would trouble relations for decades.
cia-0000124303: A November 1962 CIA technical report works out the sizes of Cosmos series satellites from their mass, area ratio, and brightness, adding matching figures for American satellites. Analysts sized up Soviet craft from the light they reflected. The paper shows technical intelligence at its most careful. Brightness tricks let analysts estimate size for craft they could never inspect, a standard method of the years before spy satellites could settle such questions directly.
cia-0000132203: Situation report 520, from January 1991, reports Israeli fears that Iraqi chemical attacks are imminent, with Israel misspelled in the original heading. Fear of gas-tipped missiles drove the handing out of gas masks. The report records that anxiety as filed. Israel's fear had deep roots in the gas attacks of the Iran war, and the sitrep's misspelling survives as a fingerprint of reporting done at crisis speed.
cia-0000132403: Cuba and Latin America are paired in a CIA document carrying an estimated date of January 1, 1961. The invasion at the Bay of Pigs was still three months away. Havana's revolution was already sending its example across the hemisphere. The short document covers that regional picture, as analysts watched governments and rebel movements react to the Cuban model in the new year.
cia-0000132503: Dissension inside Ecuador over policy toward Cuba fills a CIA document dated February 3, 1961. It pairs with a warning from the same month that violence might break out there over the same issue. The Cuba question was dividing governments and parties across the region that year. The short document tracks the Ecuadorian dispute and the sides forming within it.
cia-0000133203: Eighty-three photographs marked with the code name JMTIDE fill a CIA paper carrying an estimated date of January 1, 1961. The paper itself is untitled in the record. JMTIDE was an agency code name, and its meaning is not given here. The photographs form the picture file of some covert program. The short paper keeps the set in the bare form the record gives it.
cia-0000137003: Asylees sheltering in embassies create a dangerous problem in this June 1954 cable on extradition, signed under J. C. King. Through a channel, a request is made to resolve a tense and potentially explosive situation in Guatemala City, where diplomatic establishments including the Ecuadoran embassy hold asylees. If Ecuador refuses and insists on safe conduct, the asylees would have to be received by Ecuador, adding Iron Curtain trained communists and hardened criminals to its already alarming local communist situation. Prestige and precedent are both invoked.
cia-0000140403: Consultants for a hypnosis research project are recommended in this February 1952 memo. It discusses an unnamed psychologist known for his work in hypnosis. One researcher's ten-year experiments form a careful classic. His book is key reading for anyone serious in the field. He is now feeble and no longer interested. His two chief assistants remain active and valuable. Another man is very able and broad-minded. He has experience in research, lab, clinical, and business psychology. His judgment on hypnotism or drugs is trusted.
un-ga-res-303:
Jerusalem should belong to no single state, ruled the General Assembly in Resolution 303, adopted on 9 December 1949. The text recalls the 1947 partition vote and the 1948 vote that set up a Conciliation Commission for Palestine. Reports of that commission had been studied. The principles of the past votes, the Assembly holds, still mark a just and fair settlement of the question.

The city is to stand as a separate body under a lasting world regime. That regime must guard the Holy Places, in the city and beyond it, as the 1947 plan set out. The record's catalog year of 1947 is off; the vote is of 1949, after Israel's war of birth had left the city split in two.
un-sc-res-103:
Resolution 103 sets the terms for San Marino to join the Statute of the International Court of Justice. The Council adopted it on 3 December 1953. It acted for Japan on the same day. The vote was ten to none. The Soviet Union abstained. San Marino was a small republic. It was not a UN member at the time.

San Marino would join once it filed a signed statement with the Secretary-General. The statement also had to be ratified under its own law. In it, the republic would accept the Statute in full. It would accept the duties in Article 94 of the Charter. It would also agree to pay a fair share of the Court's costs. The Assembly would set that share after talks with its government.
un-sc-res-203: Catalogued with a 1965 date, Resolution 203 forms part of the Security Council's official record at the United Nations. These short legal texts often sit at turning points, since the Council acts when peace or security is at stake. The text here follows the English Wikisource transcription of the official record, so readers get the Council's own wording.
un-sc-res-1203: Resolution 1203 stands in the official record of the United Nations Security Council, catalogued here with a 1998 date. Such texts can call for cease-fires, set up missions, impose duties, or settle points of UN procedure and membership. Its value lies in the primary wording: the decision as adopted, kept through the Wikisource transcription of the record. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-1403: The United Nations Security Council issued Resolution 1403 as one of its formal decisions, and the catalog carries it under the year 2002. Year by year, these decisions build the written history of how the world body handled the crises of its time. The transcription keeps the preamble and numbered clauses in their official order, as the Council adopted them.
un-sc-res-1903: From 2009, Resolution 1903 is a Security Council decision kept in official-record wording via a Wikisource transcription. The members behind it acted on a peace and security question within the Council's Charter brief. Their full text is the entry: the facts as they stated them, then the measures they voted into being.
un-sc-res-2003: Resolution 2003 carries a round landmark number in the Security Council's sequence, and its official text is preserved here via Wikisource. The act itself follows the standard pattern of its kind: grounds stated, prior decisions recalled, new steps ordered in numbered form. The entry preserves the pattern and the particulars together, complete and unabridged.
cia-0000136703: A Spanish text from the 2506 Brigade documents, cataloged at 1 January 1961 with the date flagged as estimated. The new year found the brigade of anti-Castro exiles in training for a secret invasion. The record states no subject for this item. It is preserved in Spanish in the declassified release, grouped with the other estimated New Year records in the brigade's file, and described on that basis.
plos-pone-0000003:
Matthew Goddard, Jessica Leigh, Andrew Roger, and co-authors studied a selfish gene in the Cnidaria, the animal group that holds jellyfish, corals, and sea anemones. A selfish gene spreads itself through a population even when it gives the host no clear benefit. The team asked how such a gene invades and then persists.

Tracking the gene across cnidarian hosts let the authors test ideas about how these elements survive over long spans of time. Persistence is the puzzle: hosts evolve defenses, yet the gene stays. The study gives a concrete case for one of evolution's stranger claims, that selection can favor DNA that looks out only for itself.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d103: On November 8, 1943, Roosevelt wrote to Chiang Kai-shek, a fortnight before the Cairo Conference. The letter is Document 103 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Cairo would be Chiang's one summit as an equal among the great powers, and Washington's letters that month steadied the plan. The record gives the date and the names and no subject. The text is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d203:
President Roosevelt wrote to Prime Minister Churchill on 10 November 1943 about a secret bombing project aimed at Japan. New American heavy bombers, he explains, could strike early the next year from bases near Chengtu in China, hitting the coke that fed half of Japan's strained steel industry.

The bombers would supply themselves by air from new bases near Calcutta, without cutting into agreed airlift loads. Roosevelt asks Churchill to have the Government of India give every help in building four long-range bomber bases there, with American engineer troops sent as a first priority. A matching plea went to Chiang Kai-shek for five forward bases in the Chengtu area, paid for with Lend-Lease funds.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d303:
Secretary of State Cordell Hull sent President Roosevelt a secret telegram from Washington on 24 November 1943 reporting George Kennan's two-hour talk with Portuguese leader Salazar the day before. Kennan had presented Roosevelt's personal letter of 4 November, which Hull says plainly made a deep impression.

Salazar could not answer offhand, but he was not hostile. He had expected American forces to use the Azores facilities granted to Britain without asking leave. He also floated a device for the Terceira airport. Ferry aircraft might count as British from departure until past Portuguese soil, crews and engineers included. Wider facilities he equated with Portugal entering the war, which he questioned. Kennan judges the reaction encouraging and Salazar open, once a formula can square American use with Portuguese neutrality.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d403: Ambassador Alexander Kirk sent Harry Hopkins a secret, urgent telegram from Cairo on 1 December 1943. Kirk has received an urgent but garbled message from Ambassador Steinhardt at Ankara, and can only piece together its sense. From what he can gather, Steinhardt wishes Hopkins informed of two things. Neither Steinhardt nor the British ambassador at Ankara has received any message from the Tehran party. And Steinhardt believes communications from Tehran may be temporarily suspended.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d503:
President Roosevelt wrote again to Marshal Stalin on December 6, 1943, the day the Second Cairo Conference closed. The two men had parted at Tehran five days earlier after their first meeting. The State Department printed this further message in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Keeping Stalin informed was a deliberate policy: Roosevelt believed the alliance depended on the Soviet leader hearing decisions from him directly. A message sent as Cairo ended fits that pattern of prompt, personal reporting between summits. For readers, it shows the work of alliance management continuing between the famous photographs, in a correspondence that both sides watched with great care.
frus-1944-quebec-d103:
Roosevelt sent Churchill another message on August 31, 1944. The State Department printed it in the Quebec 1944 volume. The leaders exchanged several letters at the month's end. Each one narrowed the questions awaiting them in Canada.

Multiple messages in two days show business moving by topic. Some points could close by letter between the leaders. Others were marked for talks at Quebec City. The conference would open on September 12, 1944. For readers, this message adds one more piece to that preparation. It shows two heads of government clearing their desks together. It is one of several letters dated August 31 in the file.
frus-1944-quebec-d203:
Morgenthau's diary entry for September 15, 1944, quoted by the editors, captures how the zones decision was made. Leahy told him that afternoon that Roosevelt and Churchill had settled which parts of Germany each army would occupy. That morning, Morgenthau had found the president alone with a map of Europe and three colored pencils, sketching the lines himself.

Roosevelt called the Combined Chiefs' map terrible. In the afternoon he showed Churchill his own map and, in Leahy's words, got what he wanted. Leahy was happy when he read the Ruhr and Saar memorandum, Morgenthau added, because the British were going to occupy those regions and would have to carry the program out.
frus-1944-quebec-d303: Dated 18 March 1944 in its reference, this editorial note appears as document 303 near the end of the Quebec volume. The Foreign Relations editors used such notes to connect the September conference papers with earlier records from the same year. It is a guidepost rather than a wartime message, written by the Office of the Historian for later readers of the series.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d103:
Military teamwork had outrun political teamwork, this briefing book paper warns. Headed “[Liberated Countries],” it was prepared for the President's trip and is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Its subject is the need for the three chief allies to agree on one political program for freed Europe.

The allies matched their strategy for beating Germany, the paper says, but never their politics. The result is an Anglo-Soviet rivalry and a scramble for position across the continent. Each camp fears the other is planting hostile governments, right-wing in one telling, left-wing and totalitarian in the other. The paper calls the failure a real danger, both to allied unity in the war and to any stable peace.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d203:
Churchill showed Roosevelt his answer to Stalin on 6 December 1944. His message number 846, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, quotes the reply in full. It covers de Gaulle's two Moscow questions, the pact and the Rhine.

On the pact, London has no objection whatever to a Franco-Soviet treaty like its own with Moscow. Better still, Churchill floats a three-way treaty joining all three allies on identical terms, each one's duties bound to the others. On the Rhine, he says such choices should await the peace table. Yet when the three heads of government meet, they can come much closer to conclusions than they have so far.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d303:
Eden reported his Malta talks with Stettinius to Churchill on 1 February 1945, and Poland heads the account. His minute, marked P. M. (A) 2, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. The two foreign ministers had found themselves close together, and the paper sets out their shared line for Yalta.

Neither government, they agree, can recognize the Lublin government, and a solution must be found. Stettinius stressed that failure would greatly disturb American public opinion. It might even prejudice America's part in the world organization, a result Eden calls the likely fruit of a purely Russian solution. The two had similar ideas on the remedy. The present split, one Polish government in London and another in Lublin, must be put plainly to Stalin. A fusion of the two is probably past; a new interim body is the remedy they see.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d403:
Forty-five toasts were drunk at Stalin's dinner on February 8, 1945, and Bohlen's minutes glow with the mood. The atmosphere was most cordial, he writes, and Stalin was in excellent humor, even high spirits. Trust without verification is the failure mode, and naming it is the first step to fixing it.
arxiv-2606-05803: Good thermoelectric materials turn heat into electricity, and that needs low thermal conductivity. This paper shows strong optical-optical avoided crossings — where vibrational modes repel instead of passing through — suppress heat flow in gallium-substituted TlInTe2. The mechanism points toward designing better heat-to-power materials from their phonon spectra.
arxiv-2606-06103: Medical image segmentation models fail when moved to new hospitals — different scanners, different patients. MS-DKC is a dataset knowledge card framework for designing and adapting those models: cards documenting what each dataset contains and demands. Knowledge cards turn dataset roulette into informed engineering.
arxiv-2606-06303: Discrete diffusion models generate text and other discrete data, but steering them — plug-and-play guidance — is awkward. This paper does it via gradient-informed logit correction: nudging the model's scores with gradient signals. Lightweight guidance makes controllable generation practical for everyday use.
arxiv-2606-06403: Lens spaces are 3D shapes built by gluing — and equivariant eta invariants detect their subtle asymmetries. This paper develops second-jet equivariant eta separations on them: finer invariants from deeper geometric data. Sharper invariants distinguish shapes that cruder tools confuse.
arxiv-2606-06603: Particle physicists unfold detector distortions to recover true distributions — traditionally in bins. This paper does unbinned unfolding with reweighting adversarial networks. Bin-free unfolding preserves every drop of experimental information. Adversarial reweighting handles detector distortions directly. The result is cleaner physics from the same collisions.
arxiv-2606-06703: The Sun's surface oscillates, and SDO/HMI and GONG both measure it — but their Dopplergrams disagree on phases and acoustic travel times. This paper measures those inconsistencies between the two instruments. Reconciling them matters for everything helioseismology claims about the solar interior.
arxiv-2606-06803: Storage rings trap unwanted electromagnetic modes — and characterizing them matters. This paper fits long-range wake potentials with particle swarm optimization for trapped-mode parameters in the HALF ring. The fitting keeps the accelerator's beams stable. Stable beams mean better science.
arxiv-2606-06903: Animating characters usually needs skeletons — rigid bone structures. This paper goes beyond skeletons: learning animation directly from driving videos with a Same2X training strategy. The method transfers motion without ever building a rig. Video becomes the puppet master behind the animation.
arxiv-2606-07303: Representations emerge in neural networks — but why? This bootstrap theory argues explanatory insufficiency drives representational emergence and world-model learning. The theory gives emergence a mechanism. Representational emergence finally gets a concrete mechanism. Explanatory insufficiency drives the learning. A real mechanism at last.
arxiv-2606-00003: Language models that become misaligned — can they recover on their own? This paper asks whether LLMs can self-recover after misalignment by learning from mistakes. The answer matters for AI safety. Autonomous self-recovery would transform AI safety practice. The core question is profound and urgent.
arxiv-2606-00103: Evaluating how LLMs reason interactively needs games they can actually play. This hierarchical benchmark uses executable games for that evaluation. The games reveal reasoning under interaction. Interactive games reveal reasoning strategies. Structured interaction tests true understanding. The benchmark is rigorous.
