The channel stayed open through the whole war, which was itself a kind of success.
frus-1862-d303:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State, wrote to William L. Dayton in Paris on 13 August 1862, in a dispatch printed as Document 303 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Mid-August found the armies moving toward the second Bull Run campaign and foreign capitals recalculating. France's emperor was the war's most dangerous watcher, since he alone seemed eager to act. Seward's steady flow of letters to Dayton in these weeks had one aim. It was to raise the cost of French action by showing a Union that meant to fight on. Southern agents were active in Paris too, seeking loans, ships, and friends at court.
frus-1862-d403:
On 23 June 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent fresh instructions to Horace J. Perry at the Madrid legation. The letter is Document 403 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department's printed record for the year.

Midsummer 1862 was a tense season abroad. France was drifting toward deeper designs on Mexico, and Spain's next step there was unclear. From Madrid, Perry could report on both Spanish policy and French moves. Orders from Washington in these weeks kept him pressing for Spain's strict neutrality and for fair treatment of Union ships and trade in Spanish ports.
frus-1862-d503:
On 28 May 1862 James Shepherd Pike reported from The Hague to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is Document 503 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, accompanying the annual message.

Pike's late-May report came as French intentions in Mexico grew clearer. Spain was stepping back from that venture at the same time. Every American post in Europe was tracking those shifts. The Dutch watched the same board from a trader's seat. His letter gave Seward the Hague reading of a changing month. Ministers also reported the personal side of their posts: who was rising, who was ill, who had been rude. Those touches, scattered through Pike's file, make the volume's Dutch section read like a working diary of wartime diplomacy.
frus-1862-d603:
On 22 May 1862 Spain's minister of state wrote to the Spanish minister plenipotentiary serving in Mexico. The letter is Document 603 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, in the Spanish appendix.

By May, Spanish troops had left Mexico after the victory of the republic's arms at Puebla. Spain's man on the spot needed fresh guidance. He had to deal with both the Juárez government and the advancing French. Madrid's instruction, printed in translation, shows Spain redefining its Mexican position in real time. For American readers then and now, the letter completes a rare arc. The volume carries Spain's Mexican policy from the expedition's orders in December. It carries it to its winding down by summer.
frus-1862-d703:
On 4 June 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles N. Riotte, the American minister in Costa Rica. The letter is document 703 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862. It answers Riotte's report of the month before.

Seward's letters to small posts carried the same care as those to London or Paris. For Central America, Washington watched the transit routes across the isthmus and the feuds of the small republics near them. This letter shows the State Department keeping a lone envoy in line and informed. The war at home left few hands for such work at the time.
frus-1863p1-d103:
Seventh in the great batch of 2 March 1863 is this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams. Adams was the American minister in London. This letter is document 103 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, seventh in the batch.

Short sheets on set heads were how Washington ran a brief by sea mail. Each of the twelve could be filed, read, and used on its own. This one holds the seventh place in the set. For a reader now, the batch as a whole is the find. It is a full map of what the Union wanted from Britain, drawn in one day.
frus-1863p1-d203:
Washington's orders to London on 19 May 1863 came in this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 203 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

Seward wrote in a firm tone but had to avoid pushing Britain into the war on the Southern side. His instructions walked that line again and again. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d303:
Writing from London on 1 October 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. The dispatch is document 303 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

Public meetings across Britain, many of them backing the Union and emancipation, formed part of the picture Adams reported. He tracked opinion as carefully as he tracked ministers. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d403:
The American answer to London on 24 February 1863 took the form of this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 403 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Lyons was the man Seward had to persuade, warn, or answer in person in Washington. Notes to him carried the American side of each dispute between the two governments. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d503:
Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington received a letter dated 9 May 1863 from William H. Seward, Secretary of State. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily.

None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. The day-to-day work was unglamorous: answering complaints, passing on claims, and keeping track of ships, prisoners, and papers. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d603:
Under the date 5 August 1863, the record holds a letter from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad.

Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
plos-pbio-0020003:
Sophie I. Candille, Catherine D. Van Raamsdonk, Changyou Chen, and co-workers studied mouse coat color in PLOS Biology in 2004. Many mice have a light belly and a dark back. The team tied that top-to-bottom pattern to a gene called Tbx15.

Tbx15 helps set up body plans as an embryo grows. The study shows it also shapes where dark and light hair form along the back and belly. That is a neat case of one gene doing pattern work in both the body plan and the skin. The finding helps explain how animals gain their markings. It also links coat pattern to deeper rules of growth that shape the whole animal.
plos-pbio-0020203:
Edan Foley and Patrick H. O'Farrell ran a genome-wide screen of fly immunity in PLOS Biology in 2004. They silenced genes one by one in fly cells, then exposed the cells to bacteria. Genes whose loss changed the defense response were flagged for a closer look.

A screen like this turns a vague trait, innate immunity, into a list of working parts. The hits included genes no one had tied to defense before. Each one is a lead for deeper study in flies and, by comparison, in humans. Innate immunity is our first line against infection, and its fly version is close enough to ours to make such lists valuable.
plos-pbio-0020303:
Naomi Ward, Øivind Larsen, James Sakwa, and a huge team sequenced a methane-eating bacterium in PLOS Biology in 2004. Methylococcus capsulatus, called Bath, lives on methane as its sole food. Its full genome shows the tools it uses to do that rare trick.

Methane is a strong greenhouse gas, and microbes that eat it blunt its rise. The genome reveals genes for trapping methane, handling its toxic by-products, and taking up metals the process needs. That blueprint guides work on using such bacteria to cut methane from farms, landfills, and gas leaks. It also informs the search for life signs on other worlds, where methane plays a key role.
plos-pbio-0020403:
Barış Genç, P. Hande Özdinler, April E. Mendoza, and their team traced nerve fiber guidance in PLOS Biology in 2004. Proprioceptive nerves carry signals from muscles that tell the brain where limbs are. As embryos grow, those fibers must find their way into the spinal cord and to the right targets.

A factor called NT-3 acts as an attractant for these fibers, the team found. Without its pull, the fibers stray. Guidance cues like NT-3 are the road signs of the growing nervous system. Mapping them one by one explains how precise wiring arises. It also informs efforts to regrow nerves after spinal injury. The adult cord lacks those youthful signs.
plos-pone-0000103:
Jian Li, Samuel M. McClure, and Brooks King-Casas studied economic choices over time in PLOS ONE in 2006. In their game, players adjusted their strategy as conditions changed, much as governments adjust policy in a shifting economy. The authors tracked how people update their approach after wins and losses.

People did not simply chase the last good result. Their adjustments followed patterns that simple learning rules only partly capture. Games like this are the lab bench of neuroeconomics, the study of how brains make value choices. Knowing how strategies drift in dynamic settings matters for real policy too, where each new rule changes the game it governs.
plos-pone-0000203:
Jittima Piriyapongsa and I. King Jordan published this genomics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. MicroRNAs are tiny regulators that fine-tune gene activity. The authors identify a family of human microRNA genes that arose from miniature inverted-repeat transposable elements, small pieces of jumping DNA known as MITEs.

Genes born from jumping DNA show how genomes recycle their own clutter into working parts. The paper traces this family's origin and spread in the human genome. It adds to the evidence that transposable elements, often dismissed as junk, are a real source of new regulatory genes.
plos-pone-0000303:
Christian G. Noble and Haiwei Song published this molecular biology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. eIF4AIII is an RNA helicase, a motor that unwinds RNA, and a core part of a complex that marks newly made messages. The authors show that the protein MLN51 stimulates that helicase activity.

A stimulator that speeds the motor changes how the marking complex does its job in quality control of gene messages. The paper defines MLN51's role in that machinery. Such detail feeds into the study of diseases where RNA processing goes wrong. Details like these fill in the wiring of a core cellular machine.
plos-pone-0000403:
Abhaya V. Kulkarni, Jason W. Busse, and Iffat Shams asked what makes a medical paper get cited, in a 2007 PLOS ONE study. Citations are the currency of science: a paper that others cite shapes the field, while an ignored one sinks. The team looked for traits of papers that are linked to a higher citation rate.

Knowing which features go with influence helps readers judge a crowded literature and helps researchers report work so it can be found and used. The study is a piece of meta-research, science studying its own habits. Its lessons apply to anyone trying to tell landmark studies from the mass of published work.
plos-pone-0000503:
David C. Nickle and colleagues built statistical models of how HIV proteins change over time, described in PLOS ONE in 2007. HIV evolves fast, dodging immune attack and drugs. Their HIV-specific probabilistic models of protein evolution capture the virus's particular patterns of mutation, which differ from the generic models borrowed from other organisms.

A model tuned to the virus reads its sequences more accurately, spotting which changes are meaningful. That helps in tracing transmission, predicting drug resistance, and designing vaccines against a moving target. The work is infrastructure for HIV research: better math underneath many other studies.
plos-pone-0000603:
Clara S.M. Tang and Richard J. Epstein reported an unexpected division in human DNA structure, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper titled A Structural Split in the Human Genome. The genome is usually described by its sequence of letters; structure here refers to larger-scale organization in how that sequence is arranged.

A split in genome structure, if real, divides the genome into two kinds of territory with different rules. Claims of large-scale order matter because they affect how genes are regulated and how variation is distributed. Short structural papers like this one stake a claim that later genome-wide data can confirm or dissolve.
plos-pone-0000703:
Hiroki Nagai and Guojun Sheng watched two chicken globin genes switch on together, writing in PLOS ONE in 2007. The chicken beta globin locus holds four genes. Two of them, called rho and epsilon, are expressed from the earliest stage of primitive hematopoiesis, the first wave of blood formation in the embryo. The pair sits side by side in the genome.

The authors show the two genes' transcription runs in on and off phases. During each on phase, they are cotranscribed, copied together in a shared burst. That coordination raises questions about how neighboring genes share control machinery. Blood development is a classic system for gene regulation, and this adds timing to the picture.
plos-pone-0000803:
Katsuyuki Hotta, Toshio Ogura, Kenji Nishii and colleagues evaluated a blood test for tuberculosis screening in Japanese healthcare students. The whole blood interferon-gamma assay, QuantiFERON-TB-2G, had not been fully evaluated as a baseline screening test in students about to begin clinical contact with patients. Their 2007 PLOS ONE aim was to compare the assay's results with those of the tuberculin skin test.

Baseline screening matters because healthcare workers face TB exposure, and a starting value separates old infection from new. A blood test avoids return visits and reading errors of skin tests. The comparison in a low-risk student population tests the assay where false positives hurt most.
plos-pone-0000903:
Sheila Costford, Nihan Kavaslar, Nadav Ahituv and colleagues studied a human gene change that boosts a key energy enzyme, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The enzyme, AMPK, watches over energy balance in cells and in the whole body. In muscle, switching it on guards against some effects of inactivity and poor diet.

The change they studied, called R225W, sits in the gamma 3 part of AMPK and makes it work harder. The title links it to more glycogen and less fat stored in skeletal muscle. Human cases like this are rare natural tests of what a drug target does. They show both the promise and the reach of AMPK in daily metabolism.
plos-pone-0001003:
Tom Little, Lenny Nelson and Ted Hupp found signs of fast evolution in a stress response protein, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Some cancers grow from a mix of tissue damage, germs and local immune attack. The links in that chain are only starting to be unraveled.

Against that background, the team report a strong signature of adaptive evolution on the DNA sequence of a stress response protein. A sequence that changed faster than chance suggests it was shaped by real pressure, not drift. Which pressure, infection or damage, becomes the next question. The find ties an evolutionary pattern to a protein with a foot in cancer biology.
plos-pone-0001103:
Hiroyuki Kurata, Takayuki Tanaka and Fumitaka Ohnishi worked out how to find the critical reactions in a feedback rich cell model, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Computer simulations are needed to see how biochemical networks stay robust under stress or mutation. Sensitivity analysis links that robustness to network structure, but it usually gives only local answers.

The authors present a mathematical method to identify critical reactions in the interlocked feedback model, a standard test network full of loops. Reactions that carry robustness are the ones drugs and mutations hit hardest. A method that finds them reliably helps modelers spend experiments where they count.
plos-pone-0001203:
Knowing which genes are on in each tissue is basic reference data for biology. Henrik Hornshøj and colleagues built such a reference for the pig in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Using gene expression microarrays, they profiled 20,000 genes across 23 healthy porcine tissues.

Most microarray studies chase genes tied to a disease or a stimulus. A catalogue of normal expression across many tissues is a different kind of resource: the baseline against which abnormal patterns stand out. Pigs are also a major model for human medicine and a food animal, so the profiles serve several fields at once.
plos-pone-0001303:
Knocking out a gene in a mouse and measuring which other genes change activity is a standard way to find a protein's targets. Luis Valor and Seth Grant report a caution about that method in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Using tissues from multiple lines of knockout mice, they found that gene expression changes cluster around the targeted gene's location.

Changes near the manipulated locus may reflect the engineering itself rather than the missing protein's function. The authors describe these clustered changes flanking targeted gene loci. Their warning affects how thousands of microarray studies in mutant organisms should be read.
plos-pone-0001403:
Ludovic Tailleux and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study that reads both sides of a TB infection at once. Gene chips let labs watch many genes switch on or off in a sample. The team used them on the TB germ and on the human cells it infects. No prior study had read both partners in this paired way.

Their paired reads map the cross talk as germ and host react to each other. Some host genes rose while germ genes shifted to meet the new state. A two sided map like this can reveal weak points on both sides. Those weak points may yield new drug or shot targets for a disease that still kills widely.
plos-pone-0001503:
Hilde Krol and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a class of brain ills tied to a stretched protein tract. In these ills, a tract of one building block grows too long in a protein. Brains show clumps of the stretched protein, which were thought to drive harm. The team tracked one such protein, ataxin-1, live in cells.

They found the stretched protein moves faster, not slower, in cells. It also did not form clumps in their tests. That breaks the simple clump tale for this protein. Harm may come from the free protein's acts, not from clumps, which shifts drug aims.
plos-pone-0001603:
Heungjeong Woo and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a mouse model of salmonella gut ill. Mice fed salmonella by mouth do not get diarrhea as people do. A dose of germ drugs first makes them prone to gut inflammation, but gene prone mice die of body wide infection first. The team built a model in hardy mice that get the gut ill.

Their mice show diarrhea with the gut harm, much like human cases. A model that mirrors the human course lets labs test vaccines and drugs with more faith. It also helps sort gut harm from body wide spread, two ills with unlike needs.
plos-pone-0001703:
Koichi Iijima, Hsueh-Cheng Chiang, Stephen A. Hearn, and their co-authors used fruit flies to test Alzheimer's-linked protein variants in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Clumping of the amyloid-beta-42 peptide in the brain is a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease, and stopping clumping is a proposed treatment. Yet the peptide can form several kinds of assemblies, not all equally harmful.

The team made Aβ42 mutants with different aggregation profiles and expressed them in Drosophila. Different variants induced distinct pathologies in the flies, per the paper's title. The full text gives the variants, the fly brain damage, and the behavior effects. Separating which assemblies hurt most sharpens the target for anti-amyloid drugs, a field with many failed trials.
plos-pone-0001803:
Takeshi Nagashima, Takahiro Suzuki, Shinji Kondo, and their co-authors profiled gene activity in breast cancer cells in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Heregulin beta-1 is a signal that activates MAPK and PI3K/Akt pathways through ErbB receptors. Those pathways can add phosphate tags to the estrogen receptor at one site, Ser-118. That raises the question of how much the estrogen receptor matters in the response.

Their gene activity analysis shows heregulin can drive genes without the estrogen receptor in MCF-7 cells. The full text gives the gene sets and the pathway tests. If heregulin drives genes without the estrogen receptor, hormone blocking breast cancer drugs may leave this route open, which matters for resistant tumors.
plos-pone-0001903:
Jenia Semyonov and colleagues asked which gene families survive genome doubling, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. At rare points in the past, whole genomes were copied at once, leaving most genes in pairs. Most spare copies are lost with time, yet some families keep theirs far more often than chance would suggest.

The team reports that genes for G protein-coupled receptors, a huge family of cell signal catchers, are kept at high rates after such doublings. That bias hints that extra copies of signal genes paid off in survival. The work helps explain how complex signal webs grew, and why some gene families are so large today.
plos-pone-0002003:
Elie Aoun and co-authors pooled past studies to decode a gene risk in a pancreas illness, in a 2008 PLOS ONE meta-analysis. Chronic pancreatitis is long-term inflammation of the pancreas with lasting harm. One gene form, the SPINK1 N34S haplotype, marks high risk, but how it interacts with trypsin-driven injury and alcohol-driven injury was undefined.

The team set out a model in which the illness can arise by several paths, then tested it against pooled data. Sorting paths matters, since care for an alcohol-driven case may differ from care for a gene-driven one. The study gives doctors a frame for a mixed-cause illness.
plos-pone-0002103:
Sara Thomas and co-authors read the genome of a versatile soil bacterium, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Anaeromyxobacter dehalogenans strain 2CP-C is a delta-proteobacterium found in many soils and sediments. Its ribosomal RNA gene groups it with the myxobacteria, social bacteria with striking traits, yet its genome is a mosaic of pieces from many sources.

As the title states, that mosaic suggests an aerobic common ancestor for the delta-proteobacteria, a group now rich in oxygen-shunning forms. A patchwork genome can record a past way of life that the modern cell has left behind.
plos-pone-0002203:
Isabelle George, Hugo Cousillas, and Jean-Pierre Richard looked for the brain basis of sound grouping in songbirds, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Sorting sounds into classes is basic to thought, but finding where the brain does it is hard. Songbirds are a good test case because they sort songs and calls and learn them socially.

The team searched for a neural substrate, a brain area whose activity matches the sorting of complex acoustic signals into functional classes. A songbird that treats some calls as one kind and others as another must have circuitry that draws those lines. Locating it would link animal communication to the wider science of categorization.
plos-pone-0002303:
Thilo Lange, Kyu Kwang Kim, Rakesh Singh, and co-authors tested an iron-based compound against hard-to-treat ovarian cancer cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Some ovarian cancers resist platinum drugs, the standard chemotherapy, leaving few options. The compound, iron(III)-salophene, is an organometallic molecule, built around a metal atom.

In this first study of its biological activity, the team measured its effects on viability, shape, growth. Cell cycle in platinum-resistant ovarian cancer cell lines. The compound showed selective cytotoxic and anti-proliferative effects, killing cancer cells more than ordinary ones. Early selectivity like this is what drug hunters look for before animal tests.
plos-pone-0002403:
Painter joined co-authors to publish a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. Named on the byline are Corrie A. Painter, Anthony Cruz, Gustavo E. López, among others. Its subject is model for the Peptide-Free Conformation of Class II MHC Proteins. Major histocompatibility complex proteins are believed to undergo significant conformational changes concomitant with peptide binding, but structural characterization of these changes has remained elusive.

The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002503:
Ma led the team behind a 2008 research article in PLOS ONE. Named on the byline are Yanqing Ma, Craig C. Malbon, David L. Williams, among others. Its subject is altered Gene Expression in Early Atherosclerosis Is Blocked by Low Level Apolipoprotein E. Mice deficient in apolipoprotein E (apoE −/−) develop atherosclerosis.

The possible linkage between expression of adhesion molecules/cofactors and atherosclerosis was probed at the level of mRNA and protein expression. The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time.
plos-pone-0002603:
Fishman and other authors present their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Named on the byline are Yelena Fishman, Eliahu Zlotkin, Daniel Sher, among others. Its subject is expulsion of Symbiotic Algae during Feeding by the Green Hydra – a Mechanism for Regulating Symbiont Density?. Algal-cnidarian symbiosis is one of the main factors contributing to the success of cnidarians, and is crucial for the maintenance of coral reefs.

The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full.
plos-pone-0002703:
Xincheng Zheng and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was modulation of NKT cell development by B7-CD28 interaction: an expanding horizon for costimulation. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Xincheng Zheng, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. It has been demonstrated that the development of NKT cells requires CD1d. It goes on to note a further point. The contribution of costimulatory molecules in this process has not been studied. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002803:
Qingfa Wu and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008 on poly A- transcripts expressed in HeLa cells. The catalog record names Qingfa Wu first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Transcripts expressed in eukaryotes are classified as poly A+ transcripts or poly A- transcripts based on the presence or absence of the 3′ poly. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002903:
Kamija Phiri, Job Calis, Brian Faragher and colleagues followed Malawian children after severe anaemia in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Severe anaemia is common in African children admitted to hospital and often proves fatal. What happens to survivors over the long term was unknown when the study began.

Early reports had warned that survivors might face later illness and death. The team tracked outcomes to test that concern with real follow-up data. Child health programs in Africa can use such results to decide whether care should extend well past discharge from hospital. The full text gives methods, results, and references for readers who want to check each step.
plos-pone-0003003:
Suraiya Rasheed, Jasper Yan, Alex Lau and co-authors profiled proteins in HIV-infected cells in 2008. People with HIV develop metabolic problems including insulin resistance, fat redistribution, and abnormal blood lipids. These were tied to antiretroviral drugs, yet infected individuals also showed changes beyond drug effects.

Using proteomics, the team reports HIV replication itself raises free fatty acids, low density lipoproteins, and many key lipid metabolism proteins. Published in PLOS ONE, that shifts part of the blame from drugs to the virus. It may change how metabolic care for HIV patients is planned. Readers can follow the full methods and data in the complete text of the article.
plos-pone-0003103:
Ching-Shan Chou, Qing Nie and Tau-Mu Yi modeled yeast cell polarization under spatial gradients in 2008. Cells polarize by localizing internal components to specific locations in response to external signals. Yeast, for example, forms a mating projection toward the source of mating pheromone, a chemical gradient.

Polarization raises specific challenges in robustness: cells must aim accurately despite noise. The model weighs tradeoffs between robustness goals, per the title. Published in PLOS ONE, those tradeoffs are general design principles for any cell that must sense a faint gradient, from immune cells to neurons. Readers can follow the full methods and data in the complete text of the article.
plos-pone-0003203:
Jacqueline Chevalier and co-authors track a drug pump in hospital germs in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Deaths from infectious disease are set to rise as germs evolve resistance to antibiotics faster. Each new defence germs gain wears down the drugs doctors can use. Pumps that throw drugs out of the cell are one such defence.

The team compare the pump in strains of Enterobacter aerogenes taken from patients in 1995 and in 2003. Readers see how the pump changed over eight years of drug use. That record shows how treatment itself can breed harder infections.
plos-pone-0003303:
Paul C. Sereno, Ricardo N. Martinez, Jeffrey A. Wilson and colleagues report a new predatory dinosaur from Argentina in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Living birds possess a unique heterogeneous pulmonary system composed of a rigid, dorsally anchored lung and several compliant air sacs that operate as bellows, driving inspired air through the lung. Evidence from the fossil record for the origin and evolution of this system is essential.

The authors present evidence for avian intrathoracic air sacs in this new dinosaur. Readers see the bird breathing system traced into a meat-eating dinosaur. That supports a deep origin of bird-style breathing before flight itself evolved.
plos-pone-0007403: Sepsis from bacterial infections kills millions, and much of the damage comes from the body's own overreaction to a bacterial toxin called LPS. This study designed TOY, a decoy version of the immune sensor TLR4 that soaks up the toxin before it can trigger the alarm. In tests, the decoy blunted the deadly cascade behind Gram-negative sepsis, a promising new angle for treatment.
plos-pone-0007503: Long-lived industrial chemicals like DDT breakdown products have been tied to type 2 diabetes, but it was unclear which came first. This case-control study measured past exposure to the DDT metabolite p,p'-DDE in people who later developed diabetes. The link held, suggesting the pollutant itself raises diabetes risk rather than merely accompanying it.
plos-pone-0007603: Chikungunya virus swept Réunion Island in 2005–2006, sickening hundreds of thousands. This prospective study followed patients through the acute phase of infection, documenting symptoms and course. The detailed clinical picture from a massive real-world outbreak guides how doctors recognize and manage the disease.
plos-pone-0007703: A chemical that causes skin allergy was thought to work through cells alone — but this study found antibodies play a role too. In mice, specific antibodies contributed to the dermatitis triggered by dinitrochlorobenzene. The result revises the textbook picture of contact hypersensitivity.
plos-pone-0007803: Toll-like receptors are the immune system's early-warning sensors, and humans carry many variants. This study surveyed the allelic diversity of TLR genes across people. The heterogeneous repertoire shows how evolution arms populations against diverse threats.
plos-pone-0007903: Did the ancient Greeks align their temples to the stars? This survey of archaic and classical temples in Sicily tested the astronomical-orientation hypothesis. The measurements bring data to a debate that has run on speculation.
plos-pone-0008003: Cancer's tiny RNAs got a ranking hunt. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Navon's team ranked microRNAs by expression shifts across cancers. Patient-to-patient noise confounds the hunt. The ranked hits were mapped. The hunt feeds cancer genomics.
plos-pone-0008103: Mice lacking the PDZK1 protein — a regulator of the good-cholesterol receptor — suffered clogged coronary arteries and heart attacks on a fatty diet. This study links the scaffold protein to cardiovascular protection. The finding nominates a new player in heart disease.
plos-pone-0008203: A lung germ's slime switch got a mutation story. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Moyano and Smania showed mucA mutagenesis drives mucoid conversion in Pseudomonas. The biased-mutation mechanism was mapped. The story feeds cystic-fibrosis science.
plos-pone-0008303: Fusing cells were seen sharing their scaffolds. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Fant's team found non-muscle nuclei grab centrosome proteins after fusing with differentiating myoblasts. dead-men-tell-no-tales-pg1703: E. W. Hornung's 1899 adventure novel opens with a shipwreck and a survivor who may not be who he claims. Hidden identities, buried secrets, and a villain unmasked drive this non-Raffles thriller. Full of suspense: ripping Edwardian adventure from a master storyteller.
history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-volum: Volume three: the young Frederick, the attempted escape, and the execution of his friend Katte. Carlyle tells the tragedy of the prince's youth with terrible power. The making of a king through suffering, in prose like iron.
original-short-stories-volume-03: Guy de Maupassant's short stories, volume three: the French master's tales continue. Irony and pity in perfect prose. The world's greatest storyteller. Maupassant's third volume: irony and pity, the French master in fine form, perfect short fiction.
the-wandering-jew-volume-03: Eugène Sue's Wandering Jew, volume three: the plot thickens. The Jesuits close in. Suspense and sensation. The serial's early act, sue's plot thickens in volume three, the Jesuits close in, suspense grows, Sue's serial.
memoirs-of-napoleon-bonaparte-volume-03: The third volume finds Napoleon First Consul, master of France. Bourrienne records new laws, a glittering court, and the march toward empire. Peace talks and secret plots share space with daily routine. An insider's look at power taking shape.
recollections-of-the-private-life-of-nap: The third volume follows Constant through the Consulate years. Napoleon rises to supreme power while the valet keeps his quiet post. Ceremony grows grander and the court more splendid. A servant's-eye view of history turning.
essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volume-03: Volume three of the Essays ranges across Montaigne's favorite themes. He muses on custom, cruelty, and the strangeness of human nature. The tone is honest, playful, and deeply personal. A master thinking aloud on the page.
widger-s-quotations-from-the-project-gut: David Widger gathers the choicest lines from a Project Gutenberg edition. The best passages are set here side by side for easy browsing. Readers can taste the work's flavor in minutes. A handy treasury of fine writing.
coniston-volume-03: The third volume deepens the stirring political drama of Coniston. The hero's high ideals clash head-on with the party machine. New Hampshire politics turn personal, bitter, and fierce. The gathering story builds steadily toward its climax.
file-no-113-pg3803: Gaboriau's File No. 113 is a landmark of the detective novel. A daring bank robbery hides a deeper and darker secret crime. The methodical French sleuth follows the paper trail patiently. The master of the genre at his very best.
the-confessions-of-jean-jacques-rousseau: The third volume of the Confessions idylls at Les Charmettes. Rousseau's happy years with Madame de Warens glow ever brightly. Sweet nature, love, and music fill the gentle pages. The precious calm before life's great storms.
the-red-lily-volume-03: The third volume of The Red Lily deepens Therese's painful dilemma. Love and stern convention pull her in opposite directions. Anatole France's cool irony never falters for a moment. A masterpiece of French subtlety and grace.
serge-panine-volume-03: The third volume of Serge Panine tightens the net remorselessly. The adventurer's clever deceptions approach their inevitable and terrible crisis. His frightened victims begin to see the truth. Stage-worthy suspense maintained to the very final page.
monsieur-madame-and-be-be-volume-03: The third volume of Monsieur, Madame and Bebe continues the domestic comedy. The growing baby brings new joys and fresh trials to the parents. Droz's kindly humor stays ever fresh. Family life lovingly laughed at and loved.
plos-pone-0357103: A chemical tag called β-hydroxybutyrylation may reshape genes in failing hearts. This paper integrated bulk and single-cell transcriptomics to reveal its association characteristics with heart failure. The combined analysis pinpoints which cells and genes the tag touches — a new layer in heart failure biology.
plos-pone-0357303: RSV isn’t just a children’s virus — it hospitalizes older adults too. This retrospective analysis of Brazil’s surveillance database measured the burden of RSV hospitalizations among adults aged 60 and older from 2013 onward. The numbers make the case for protecting seniors with vaccines and awareness, not just infants.
plos-pone-0353503: Comparing Chinese handwriting is hard: thousands of characters, endless personal styles. This paper built character-level attention Siamese networks that learn to judge whether two handwriting samples match. The model gives forensic examiners and archivists a tireless AI second opinion on questioned documents.
plos-pone-0358103: Reading emotions in text is big business — and accuracy is everything. This paper optimized sentiment classification with improved Senti-BERT plus BiLSTM-Attention. The hybrid architecture squeezes more accuracy from the models that decide whether a review glows with praise or grumbles with complaint.
plos-pone-0357203: When medical errors harm patients, the clinicians involved become ‘second victims’ — traumatized and often unsupported. This scoping review mapped the repercussions of the second victim phenomenon on healthcare workers. The synthesis shows what these hidden victims endure and which support actually helps them recover.
plos-pone-0357803: Acne does more than scar skin — it can seed phobic anxiety that outlasts the pimples. This study at a national dermatology hospital in Vietnam measured the prevalence, clinical phenotype, and associated factors of phobic anxiety disorders among acne patients. The findings firmly link dermatology with mental health.
plos-pone-0357903: Pneumococcus still colonizes children’s noses even in the conjugate vaccine era. This Brazilian cross-sectional study measured nasopharyngeal carriage of Streptococcus pneumoniae in children aged two to five in Salvador. The carriage data track the vaccine’s real-world impact — and its limits.
plos-pone-0352103: Do liberals and conservatives express political hatred differently? This paper tested within-person effects of political attitudes on outgroup animosity, uncovering a clear Democratic-Republican asymmetry. The evidence complicates the lazy both-sides narrative with careful longitudinal data.
plos-pone-0357403: After local extinctions, mite communities on grasslands reassemble — but how, and how fast? This paper tracked the fine-scale recovery of mite communities following local extinctions. The recovery patterns reveal the hidden rules of recolonization, informing grassland restoration everywhere.
plos-pone-0356103: Methamphetamine ravages the heart, driving inflammation in cardiac tissue. This rat study tested whether endurance training reduces those inflammatory markers in meth-exposed hearts. The results suggest exercise might partially undo the drug’s cardiac damage — a hopeful lead for recovery programs.
plos-pone-0354703: Trigraphene nanosheets — three atomic layers of carbon — fail in direction-dependent ways. This molecular dynamics study probed their anisotropic fracture mechanisms and crack-mediated mechanical degradation. The atomic-scale insights guide engineers designing with these remarkable materials.
plos-pone-0357003: Tomorrow’s Sudanese doctors need solid TB knowledge today. This cross-sectional study assessed tuberculosis-related knowledge, attitudes, and self-reported preventive practices among medical students at the University of Khartoum. The educational diagnosis reveals exactly where the curriculum must improve.
plos-pone-0356003: Sub-Saharan Africa’s primary care systems must absorb chronic disease care — but how? This paper published a systematic review protocol on implementation strategies for integrating non-communicable disease care into primary healthcare. The planned synthesis will identify which integration strategies actually work in resource-constrained settings.
plos-pone-0355403: Chip seal roads need fog seal overlays that grip despite sandy contamination. This paper optimized a sand-containing fog seal overlay design using response surface methodology. The optimized formulation extends pavement life on roads that conventional seals would abandon.
plos-pone-0355603: Training text classifiers is expensive — unless you pick the most informative examples. This paper proposed a novel hybrid model for identifying the most informative instances for improving text classification. The smart sampling slashes labeling costs while boosting model performance.
plos-pone-0354103: Surgically restoring blood flow to a starving brain — revascularisation — promises recovery but needs rigorous study. This paper published the protocol for a single-arm interventional study of hemodynamic, neurological, and cognitive outcomes after surgery for occlusive cerebrovascular disease. The planned research will quantify what revascularisation truly restores.
plos-pone-0353903: Mexican older adults’ intrinsic capacity — what their bodies and minds can do — reflects social vulnerability. This paper drew on the 2021 Mexican Health and Aging Study to examine those health determinants. The findings link social conditions to biological aging — demanding policies that address both.
plos-pone-0355503: The Changshan waterway — how many vessels can it safely pass? This paper researched its vessel passing capacity. The capacity analysis informs the shipping schedules and infrastructure investments that keep this aquatic artery flowing.
plos-pone-0355203: Measuring multiphase flow — oil, gas, water together — under noisy industrial conditions is brutally hard. AUKF-PINN is an adaptive framework for low-energy gamma multiphase flow measurement in such environments. The physics-informed AI promises accurate flow metering where conventional sensors drown in noise.
plos-pone-0355303: Extracellular vesicles in liver tissue fluid carry non-coding RNAs with diagnostic promise. This paper optimized their extraction from hepatic interstitial fluid and analyzed ncRNA expression profiles. The methodological advance opens a new window on liver disease — through the vesicles tissues shed.
plos-pone-0355103: Asthma, eczema, and multiple sclerosis — did the pandemic shift their incidence? This U.S. claims database study tracked trends before, during, and after COVID-19. The findings reveal whether pandemic disruptions — or the virus itself — altered the trajectory of three major immune-mediated diseases.
plos-pone-0354903: Dialysis devours water, energy, and generates waste — Türkiye’s footprint was unmeasured until now. This national scenario-based analysis quantified the environmental cost of in-center hemodialysis. The findings confront nephrology with its ecological bill — and the greener scenarios that could shrink it.
plos-pone-0354603: AI grading pronunciation — alongside humans — raises questions of reliability and bias. This paper examined scoring reliability and bias in human versus generative AI pronunciation assessment. The findings test whether machines judge language learners fairly — or encode new inequities.
plos-pone-0354803: Permanent magnet synchronous motors — controlling them without exact models — is the promise of model-free predictive control. This paper built it on nonlinear autoregressive exogenous models with adaptive recursive least squares. The findings bring robust motor control to applications where precise modeling is impossible.
plos-pone-0354303: Sorbus tianschanica seedlings — Tian Shan rowan — respond to light quality. This paper measured growth and photosynthetic effects. The findings guide nursery practice for a mountain tree — light recipes for healthy seedlings.
plos-pone-0352503: G-protein coupled receptors orchestrate signaling in the brain’s substantia nigra — the region that degenerates in Parkinson’s disease. This paper mapped signal and signal-transduction related transcripts in nigral volume and pigmented neurons. The mapping revealed a potential deficit of nigral signaling machinery. That deficit could explain why these particular neurons die while neighbors survive. The findings point to GPCR pathways as therapeutic targets for Parkinson’s.
plos-pone-0350403: Germany’s AfD supporters — driven by immigration concern rather than deprivation. This paper demonstrated that distinction. The findings challenged the economic anxiety narrative of far-right support. The research reframes the populist surge — culture, not pocketbooks, as the engine — with implications for democratic responses.
plos-pone-0352203: A daily liter of plain water — intentionally — its effect on total fluid and caloric intake. This paper tested it in free-living adults. The simple intervention displaced caloric beverages. The findings validate the cheapest dietary advice — drink water — with experimental rigor.
plos-pone-0346003: Chinese vocational college administrators — their acceptance of generative AI. This UTAUT-guided thematic study explored it. The findings revealed the factors shaping adoption in career education. The research guides AI integration where it trains the workforce — the colleges building China’s skilled labor.
plos-pone-0354203: Natural-synthetic hybrid composite laminates — their mechanical performance investigated experimentally and numerically. This paper did so. The testing revealed how plant and synthetic fibers cooperate under load. The findings advanced sustainable composites — strength with a smaller footprint.
plos-pone-0353203: Respiratory waveform and rate from photoplethysmography — estimated by late fusion multi-task learning. This paper built it. The model read breathing from the pulse oximeter’s signal. The findings multiplied the wearable’s senses — breath measured where only pulse was. The late fusion is the architecture: it processes the PPG signal through separate pathways before combining them for the final estimate.
plos-pone-0353303: Old Dongola in northern Sudan — agricultural production across the fourteenth to eighteenth centuries, through the transition to Islam. This diachronic assessment asked: continuity or change? The findings tested whether religious transformation reshaped farming. The research read the fields — agriculture as the archive of cultural change.
plos-pone-0352903: Artisanal coalho cheese from the Caatinga — lactic acid bacteria diversity through metataxonomic insights. This paper did so. The findings catalogued the microbes behind Brazil’s traditional cheese. The research preserved the heritage — the Caatinga’s bacteria, named. The Caatinga biome is the terroir: the harsh Brazilian scrubland’s microbes give the cheese a character no starter culture can replicate.
plos-pone-0352703: Cardiac surgery — dynamic communication and workload patterns in an explorative study. This paper did so. The analysis mapped who talks to whom under pressure. Its safety value is the teamwork. The work listens to the operating room’s choreography. The explorative design is the honesty: it maps the territory before hypothesizing, letting the OR’s patterns emerge.
plos-pone-0348903: Iranian university students — entrepreneurship education and mindset shaping entrepreneurial intention. This paper explored how. The analysis traced the classroom to the startup dream. The finding is the influence. The work asks what makes the student dare. The Iranian context is the constraint: sanctions and culture shape what ‘entrepreneurship’ can mean there.

dieterich-mithrasliturgie-1903:
Albrecht Dieterich published his edition of the so-called Mithras Liturgy in 1903, in German. The ritual survives inside a great Greek magical papyrus from Egypt. Dieterich gave it a text, translation, and long commentary.

The rite guides a soul upward through the heavens toward the sun god. Prayers, secret names, and breath control mark the ascent's stages. Dieterich connected the text with the Mithras mysteries, a link scholars still debate. His publication changed study of ancient magic and mystery religion overnight. The liturgy remains one of the most discussed ritual texts from antiquity. Dieterich's commentary still frames the argument.
amadis-of-gaul-southey-vol1-1803:
Amadis of Gaul is the great Spanish romance of chivalry that set the pattern for a whole age of fiction. Robert Southey, the English poet, translated it, and the first volume appeared in 1803. Its hero Amadis became the model knight for readers across Europe.

Amadis loves the lady Oriana and proves himself against giants, enchanters, and rival knights. Battles, shipwrecks, and magic fill this opening volume. The book bewitched Renaissance readers, and Cervantes honored it even while mocking its imitators. Southey's version brought the Spanish epic to English readers in full. Volume one launches the quest in high style.
amadis-of-gaul-southey-vol4-1803:
Southey's Amadis of Gaul ends with this fourth volume, published in 1803. The Spanish romance had shaped European ideas of knighthood for three hundred years before Southey Englished it. Here the long tale of Amadis and Oriana reaches its close.

Final battles settle the wars that run through all four volumes. The last enchantments break, and old wrongs come right at last. The lovers win their hard reward after years of trial. With this volume ends the romance that taught Europe how to dream of knights. Its shadow falls across Don Quixote and across every chivalric tale written after it.
amadis-of-gaul-southey-vol2-1803:
Robert Southey's translation of Amadis of Gaul ran to four volumes in 1803, and this is the second. The Spanish romance follows the peerless knight Amadis, the standard by which later heroes were judged. His deeds for his lady Oriana drive the whole vast tale.

Volume two carries Amadis through wars fought for Oriana's hand and fresh dangers in strange lands. Enchantments test his faith, and new knights enter the lists beside him. The pace is pure romance, with marvel piled on marvel. Readers of Cervantes will know this world well, since Don Quixote's library was full of such books. The epic here rides at full gallop.
amadis-of-gaul-southey-vol3-1803:
The third volume of Southey's Amadis of Gaul came out in 1803 with the rest of his translation. Amadis, the Spanish knight whose fame spread over Europe, faces his hardest trials of constancy here. His lady Oriana remains the center of all his deeds.

Sorcerers lay cunning traps, and magic isles rise out of the sea to test him. Amadis must hold his faith through long separation and false reports. The wonders come thick in this book, the richest in marvels of the four. Southey, himself a poet of romance, keeps the old Spanish fire alive in English. The volume brings the epic near its climax.
harsnett-declaration-egregious-popish-im:
Samuel Harsnett, a rising churchman, published his Declaration of Egregious Popish Impostures in 1603. Its target is the Catholic exorcisms staged in England in the 1580s, which Harsnett exposes as fraud. Priests, he argues, coached the possessed and faked the devils' voices to win converts.

The book is fierce anti-Catholic polemic, and a great debunking besides. Its lists of devil names and its raving speeches had an odd afterlife. Shakespeare read it, and its language echoes in the mad scenes of King Lear. Few polemics change literature by accident. Harsnett's attack on possession stands as the classic English exposure of exorcism as theater.
jorden-suffocation-mother-1603:
Edward Jorden, a London physician, published his Briefe Discourse on the suffocation of the mother in 1603. The disease is what his age called hysteria, a disorder of the womb blamed for fits and strange symptoms. Jorden wrote after a famous case in which a girl's fits had been charged to witchcraft, and his tract intervened in that quarrel.

He argues that supposed possessions are this natural disease at work. The symptoms that looked demonic, he shows, follow the body's own patterns. His medical text quietly undercut possession claims across England. Courts and clergy had to reckon with a doctor's reading of the afflicted. Jorden's discourse remains a landmark of medicine entering the witch debate.
